i OurBigBook.com
The set difference consists of elements belonging to the first set but not the second:
A∖B={x∈U:x∈A and x∈/B}.​
(1)
The symmetric difference consists of elements belonging to exactly one of the two sets:
A⊕B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A).​
(2)
In particular, the two sets in this union are disjoint sets.

ii

Words: 66 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 66
ii OurBigBook.com
Every complement of a set is taken in the same universal set U. Apply De Morgan's laws for propositional logic to the membership propositions. For every x∈U,
x∈A∩Bx∈A∪B​⟺¬(x∈A∧x∈B)⟺(x∈/A∨x∈/B)⟺x∈A∪B,⟺¬(x∈A∨x∈B)⟺(x∈/A∧x∈/B)⟺x∈A∩B.​
(3)
Equality of membership for every element proves the set identities
A∩B=A∪B,A∪B=A∩B.​
(4)

Using set difference as an intersection with a complement of a set, and using double negation, gives
A⊕B​=(A∩B)∪(B∩A)=(B∖A)∪(A∖B)=A⊕B.​
(5)
Interchanging the two sets simply interchanges the two terms of this union, whose commutativity gives
A⊕B=A⊕B,A⊕B=B⊕A.​
(6)

ii

Words: 107 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 107
ii OurBigBook.com
We use a double inclusion proof. First, let x∈A⊕B​. If x∈A, then x∈B, since otherwise x∈A∖B⊆A⊕B. Hence in this case x∈A∩B. If x∈/A, then x∈/B, since otherwise x∈B∖A⊆A⊕B. Hence in this case x∈A∪B. This proves the first set inclusion.
Conversely, an element of A∩B belongs to neither A∖B nor B∖A. An element of A∪B also belongs to neither set difference. Thus every element of (A∩B)∪A∪B lies outside A⊕B, proving the reverse set inclusion. Therefore
A⊕B​=(A∩B)∪A∪B.​
(7)

ii OurBigBook.com
If f(x)=f(y), applying the function f gives f(f(x))=f(f(y)). Since f∘f=idA​, this implies x=y, proving injectivity. Also every y∈A is the image of f(y), because f(f(y))=y, proving surjectivity.
Thus f is a bijection and its inverse function is itself:
f−1=f.​
(9)
Such a function is an involution.

f(f(x))=c2x+(c+1)d.

Equating coefficients requires c2=a and (c+1)d=b. Because a>0 and a=1, either choice c=a​ or c=−a​ has c+1=0. Thus two valid functions are
f(x)=a​x+1+a​b​​andf(x)=−a​x+1−a​b​.​
(12)
Substitution into c2x+(c+1)d verifies each answer. These provide the requested maps; no assumption that every possible solution is affine function is needed.

There are n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1) ordered selections without replacement. Each unordered k-element subset occurs in exactly k! orders, so the binomial coefficient is
(kn​)=k!(n−k)!n!​.​
(14)
One precise specification of its domain, codomain, and map is
C:D⟶N0​,D={(n,k)∈N02​:0≤k≤n},(n,k)⟼k!(n−k)!n!​.​
(15)
Here N0​={0,1,2,…}, and 0!=1 includes the single empty selection. The actual values on D are positive, so N+​ is also a valid codomain. For fixed n, one can instead use the function Cn​:{0,…,n}→N+​ with Cn​(k)=(kn​).

(2n​)+(2n+1​)=2n(n−1)​+2n(n+1)​=n2​.

For 0≤k≤n, the adjacent binomial coefficients obey
(k+1n​)=(kn​)k+1n−k​,g(k)=(kn​)k+1n−2k−1​.
(17)
Since (kn​)>0 and k+1>0, the sign is determined by the numerator:
g(k)>0⟺0≤k<2n−1​.​
(18)
The printed codomain N+​ is inconsistent with the displayed map: g(n)=−1, and when n is odd, g((n−1)/2)=0. With the usual extension (kn​)=0 for k>n, g is a function N0​→Z, and g(k)=0 for k>n; the positive range above remains unchanged. Without that extension, the natural domain is {0,…,n}.[ref]

Solution
Words: 89
ii OurBigBook.com
In the intended range 0≤k≤n, division by the positive binomial coefficient (kn​) gives
k+1n−2k−1​=1,n=3k+2.
(19)
Consequently the intended remainder is
nmod3=2.​
(20)
There is a necessary qualification to the printed unrestricted domain. If binomial coefficients outside 0≤k≤n are extended by zero, then every k>n satisfies g(k)=(kn​)=0, regardless of nmod3. For example, n=3,k=4 satisfies the literal equality but has nmod3=0. Thus the literal extended-domain premise alone does not determine a remainder; the boxed conclusion requires 0≤k≤n, or equivalently here (kn​)=0.

For adjacent binomial coefficients, the ratio
(kn​)(k+1n​)​=k+1n−k​
(21)
is greater than 1 when k<(n−1)/2, equal to 1 at k=(n−1)/2, and less than 1 afterwards. For odd n, the row is therefore increasing up to its two equal central entries and decreasing after them. The maximum is attained exactly at
k∗=2n−1​ork∗=2n+1​.​
(22)
They are distinct, including when n=1, so k∗ is not unique. This is the unimodality of binomial coefficients.

q2=q+1.

Fn​=Aϕn+Bψn.

Use mathematical induction with two base cases. At n=0, the formula gives (1−1)/5​=0=F0​. At n=1, it gives (ϕ−ψ)/5​=1=F1​.
If it holds at n−1 and n, then the Fibonacci recurrence gives

For functions f,g:N→R, big O notation means
f=O(g)⟺∃C>0 ∃N ∀n≥N:∣f(n)∣≤C∣g(n)∣.​
(32)
Using the natural logarithm and exponential function, 3logn=nlog3. Since log3>1, for every n≥1 we have n≤nlog3. The witnesses C=1,N=1 therefore prove
n=O(3logn).​

0≤(n+3logn)2≤(2n2)2=4n4.

The definition of big O notation holds with C=4,N=1:
(n+3logn)2=O(n4).​

Suppose the definition of big O notation held with constants C>0,N. Choose an odd integer n>max(C,N). At this input, f(n)=n and g(n)=1, so the required inequality would be n≤C, a contradiction. Thus
f=O(g).​
(36)
The infinitely many even inputs, where f(n)/g(n)=1/n, cannot repair the failure on odd inputs because the bound must hold for every sufficiently large input.

Fn​=O(2n).​

The greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer dividing both inputs:
gcd(a,b)=max{d∈N+​:d∣a and d∣b}.​
(43)
This maximum exists because 1 belongs to the set and all its elements are at most b.

ii

Words: 46 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 46
ii OurBigBook.com
Write a=qb+r using the Euclidean division. If d∣a and d∣b, then d∣(a−qb)=r. Conversely, if d∣b and d∣r, then d∣(qb+r)=a. Therefore (a,b) and (b,r) have exactly the same positive common divisors, proving
gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r).​
(44)
For r=0, this agrees with gcd(b,0)=b.

Set (a0​,b0​)=(a,b). At each iteration with bi​>0, compute the remainder ri​=ai​modbi​, then set
(ai+1​,bi+1​)=(bi​,ri​).​
(45)
Stop at the first index n with bn​=0 and return an​. The positive second coordinates strictly decrease, so algorithm termination follows from the well-ordering principle. The equality of greatest common divisors established in (ii) is a loop invariant, and at termination it gives
an​=gcd(an​,0)=gcd(a,b).​
(46)

i OurBigBook.com
Consider one iteration with ai​>bi​>0 and ri​=ai​modbi​. If bi​≤ai​/2, then ri​<bi​≤ai​/2. If bi​>ai​/2, the quotient is 1, so ri​=ai​−bi​<ai​/2. In either case ri​<ai​/2, whence
ai+1​bi+1​=bi​ri​<2ai​bi​​.
(47)
Repeated application, or mathematical induction, proves
an​bn​<2nab​(n≥1 performed iterations).​
(48)
This also holds for the final iteration, whose left side is zero. For zero iterations the correct relation is equality a0​b0​=ab, rather than a strict inequality.

Words: 98 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 98
ii OurBigBook.com
Count the final division producing zero as an iteration, and let the total be n. The terminal product an​bn​=0 alone gives no useful bound. Instead apply (i) to each nonterminal product, which is a positive integer and hence at least 1.
If n≥2, the penultimate product satisfies
1≤an−1​bn−1​<2n−1ab​,n−1<log2​(ab).
(49)
As n is an integer, this implies
n≤⌈log2​(ab)⌉.​
(50)
For n=1, the same bound holds since a>b≥1 implies ab≥2. In particular the Euclidean algorithm uses O(loga+logb) divisions, in big O notation. The convention that includes the final zero-producing division explains the one-step offset in the argument.

iii

Words: 125 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 125
iii OurBigBook.com
The second coordinate after two iterations satisfies
bi+2​=bi​modbi+1​<2bi​​
(51)
whenever those two divisions are needed, by the same remainder bound, now applied to bi​>bi+1​>0. Let m=⌊log2​b⌋. If the Euclidean algorithm has not already stopped after 2m iterations, then its positive second coordinate is at most 1: for m≥1,
0<b2m​<2mb​<2.
(52)
For m=0 the original b is already 1. A second coordinate of 1 requires just one more division. Consequently
n≤2⌊log2​b⌋+1,n=O(logb) as b→∞.​
(53)
This removes dependence on the potentially much larger input a. It improves the scale log2​(ab) to one involving only the smaller input; the rounded numerical bound need not be smaller for every pair. One may always take the minimum of the bounds in (ii) and (iii).

Assume the homogeneous function is differentiable. Applying the multivariable chain rule to f(tx,ty)=tmf(x,y) gives, for t near 1,
xfx​(tx,ty)+yfy​(tx,ty)=mtm−1f(x,y).
(54)
Setting t=1 proves Euler theorem for homogeneous functions:
x∂x∂f​+y∂y∂f​=mf.​
(55)
Only positive t near 1 are needed, so the derivation remains valid even when a noninteger m makes the printed phrase “all real t” require qualification.

The linear ordinary differential equation has differential operator (D−3)2. Put y=e3xv and use the product rule twice:
y′=e3x(3v+v′),y′′=e3x(9v+6v′+v′′).
(56)
Substitution cancels the v and v′ terms, leaving v′′=4. Two integrations give v=2x2+C1​x+C2​. Hence the general solution is
y(x)=e3x(2x2+C1​x+C2​),C1​,C2​∈R.​
(57)
The two arbitrary constants account for the order of the differential equation; the x2 factor in the particular term reflects the repeated root 3 of the characteristic polynomial.

On an interval with x=0, set y=xv. The product rule gives y′=v+xv′, and substitution gives
x2(v+xv′)=x2+x2v+x2v2,xv′=1+v2.​
(58)
This is a separable differential equation. Since 1+v2>0 for real v, separation loses no real constant solution:
1+v2dv​=xdx​,arctanv=log∣x∣+C.
(59)
Thus the general solution on any interval avoiding zero and the poles of the tangent function is
y(x)=xtan(log∣x∣+C).​
(60)
At x=0 the original differential equation forces y(0)=0, but no real solution from this family extends over a whole interval through zero: log∣x∣+C encounters infinitely many poles as x→0.

For x=±1, write the linear ordinary differential equation as
y′+1−x22x​y=1−x2x(1−x)​.
(61)
An integrating factor on each interval avoiding ±1 is μ(x)=1/(1−x2); multiplication by a nonzero constant, including a sign, is immaterial. Therefore
(1−x2y​)′=(1−x2)2x(1−x)​=(1−x)(1+x)2x​.
(62)
The partial fraction decomposition is
(1−x)(1+x)2x​=4(1−x)1​+4(1+x)1​−2(1+x)21​.
(63)
Integrating gives the general solution
y(x)=21−x​+(1−x2)(C+41​log​1−x1+x​​),x=±1.​
(64)
The constant is independent on each connected interval of definition. At the singular points the undivided differential equation forces y(1)=0 and y(−1)=1. The displayed family tends to these values, but its derivative has a logarithmic divergence there, so no member extends as a differentiable function through either singular point.

The amplification factor is R=1−λ/N. To reproduce decay, the forward Euler method requires ∣R∣<1, equivalently
−1<1−Nλ​<1⟺N>λ/2.​
(73)
At N=λ/2, R=−1 and the approximations alternate with constant magnitude 2; for N<λ/2, ∣R∣>1 and the magnitude grows. This is the condition of absolute stability for this decaying differential equation.
Stability is only a minimum requirement. Values just inside the bound can still give a poor endpoint approximation; resolving the decay accurately generally requires a smaller step size. If positivity at every step is desired, the stronger condition N≥λ ensures R≥0. The figure shows the difference between decay of the exact solution and numerical oscillation.

For positive edge lengths the volume is V=abc and the surface area constraint is 2(ab+ac+bc)=S. Introduce a Lagrange multiplier μ:
L=abc−μ(2ab+2ac+2bc−S).
(74)
The stationary point equations are
bc=2μ(b+c),ac=2μ(a+c),ab=2μ(a+b).
(75)
Multiplying these by a,b,c, respectively, and equating their left sides gives μc(a−b)=0 and μb(a−c)=0. Because all edge lengths are positive, the equations imply μ>0; hence a=b=c. The constraint gives 6a2=S.
To establish a global maximum, rather than only a stationary point, apply the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to ab,ac,bc:
6S​=3ab+ac+bc​≥((ab)(ac)(bc))1/3=(abc)2/3.
(76)
Equality holds exactly when ab=ac=bc, or a=b=c. Therefore
Vmax​=(6S​)3/2,a=b=c=S/6​.​
(77)

κn​=(Lnπ​)2,Xn​(x)=Bn​sinLnπx​,n=1,2,…,Bn​=0.​

The identically zero function is also a solution. Allowing Bn​=0 includes it in the displayed family. Here L>0 is the interval length and n labels the eigenvalues of the operator −d2/dx2 with these boundary conditions.

The heat equation and its homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions are linear, so superposition of the separated modes gives
u(x,t)=n=1∑∞​αn​sinLnπx​exp(−L2Dn2π2t​).​
(87)
The Fourier sine basis represents the initial profile on the interior of the interval. At t=0 its Fourier sine series must equal x(1−x). Multiplying by sin(mπx/L), integrating from 0 to L, and using orthogonality gives
∫0L​sinLnπx​sinLmπx​dx={L/2,0,​n=m,n=m.​

Therefore the required Fourier sine coefficients are
αn​=L2​∫0L​x(1−x)sinLnπx​dx,n=1,2,….​
(89)
For every t>0, the exponential factors ensure convergence of the differentiated series, and every term satisfies the partial differential equation and the boundary conditions. The Fourier sine series recovers the smooth initial profile at every 0<x<L as t↓0.
The scan explicitly prints x(1−x) on (0,L); it must not silently become x(L−x). For L=1, the interior profile tends to L(1−L)=0 at the right endpoint, whereas the prescribed boundary condition is zero for t>0. The solution is therefore not continuous at the corner (L,0), although it satisfies every condition on the printed open ranges. A solution continuous on the closed space-time domain with these data would require L=1.[ref]

Bi​∩Bj​=∅(i=j),i⋃​Bi​=Ω.​

Let τ be the absorption time. Its expectation is finite: from every interior state, a string of at most n successive left moves reaches 0, and the probability of such a string is at least p=3−n. Hence the Markov property gives Pk​(τ>jn)≤(1−p)j, a geometric tail bound, and Ek​[τ]<∞.
For 1≤k≤n−1, one step is always spent before absorption or the remaining walk. Apply first-step analysis and the law of total expectation to the three possible first moves. The conditional expectations of the remaining absorption time are ek+1​,ek​,ek−1​, respectively; independence of future moves gives the same law as a fresh random walk from the new position. Thus
ek​=1+31​ek+1​+31​ek​+31​ek−1​,
(92)
which rearranges to
31​ek+1​−32​ek​+31​ek−1​=−1.​
(93)
The term 1 also appears when the walk stays at k, because staying still consumes a step.

The probability generating function of a nonnegative integer-valued random variable is
G(s)=E[sX]=j=0∑∞​p(j)sj.​
(100)
Use s0=1, including at s=0. The power series converges absolutely for every real s∈[−1,1], since ∑j​p(j)∣s∣j≤1. In particular it is always defined on the usual probability-generating interval [0,1]. It may also be defined for ∣s∣>1, depending on the radius of convergence and convergence at its endpoints; the precise real domain of finite expectation is {s∈R:∑j​p(j)∣s∣j<∞}.

Solution

By hypothesis the power series converges at every positive real argument, so its radius of convergence is infinite. Termwise differentiation of a power series is therefore valid in a neighborhood of s=1. For k≥1,
G(k)(s)=∑j=k∞​j(j−1)⋯(j−k+1)p(j)sj−k.
(101)
At s=1, the right side is the expectation of the falling factorial of X:
G(k)(1)=E[X(X−1)⋯(X−k+1)].​
(102)
The special case k=1 gives
G′(1)=E[X].​
(103)
For k=0, take the empty product as 1; the equality becomes G(1)=1. These are the factorial moments.

E[X2]=G′′(1)+G′(1).

Subtracting the squared mean yields the variance
var(X)=G′′(1)+G′(1)−(G′(1))2.​
(105)

E[X(X−1)⋯(X−k+1)]=1(k≥0).​

Each of the n distinguishable elements has x independent choices of colour. By the multiplication principle, the number of functions from the n-element set to the x-element colour set is
xn.​
(109)

ii

Solution
Words: 115
ii OurBigBook.com
Group the elements of a colouring by equality of colour. This creates a unique partition of a set into nonempty unlabelled blocks, each of one colour, with distinct blocks assigned distinct colours.
For a partition of a set with k blocks, assigning distinct colours to the blocks gives the falling factorial x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1) possibilities. To see that no extra factor k! is needed, order the blocks canonically by their smallest elements, then assign colours in that order. There are A(n,k) possible set partitions with k blocks; these numbers are the Stirling numbers of the second kind.
Every colouring is counted exactly once in exactly one value of k, so
xn=k=1∑n​A(n,k)x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1).​
(110)
For k>x, no colouring of the blocks is possible and the displayed falling factorial is zero, because one factor is x−x.

Using the probability mass function of the Poisson distribution directly gives
E[Xn]=e1​j=0∑∞​j!jn​.​
(111)
For each fixed positive integer n, this series converges: the ratio of successive nonzero terms is (1+1/j)n/(j+1), which tends to zero. Equivalently, using the polynomial identity in (ii) and the factorial moments from (a)(iv) gives E[Xn]=∑k=1n​A(n,k); the extension of that identity to X=0,1 is justified in (iv).

Both sides of (ii) are polynomials in the colour count, and they agree at every integer x≥2. A nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots, so this is a polynomial identity and holds also at x=0,1. It can therefore be evaluated at every possible value of the Poisson random variable X.
Take expectations and use the factorial moments from (a)(iv). The sum over k is finite, so linearity of expectation gives
E[Xn]=∑k=1n​A(n,k)E[X(X−1)⋯(X−k+1)]=∑k=1n​A(n,k)=B(n).
(112)
Combining this with (iii) proves Dobiński's formula for the Bell numbers:
B(n)=e1​j=0∑∞​j!jn​(n≥1).​
(113)
For completeness, the empty set has one partition of a set, giving B(0)=1; that case uses the empty-product conventions 00=1 in this identity and a k=0 term in the partition sum.
